# qgrid

**Maidenhead grid square calculator with a map and a compass**

- **Version recorded:** 3.2
- **Categories:** `antenna`, `hf-propagation`, `station`
- **Upstream:** <https://www.qsl.net/on4qz/qgrid/index.html>

## What it does

Converts between Maidenhead locators and latitude and longitude, computes distance and bearing between two squares, and draws the result -- a map with the path on it and a compass rose showing the heading. It will take a list of squares and work through them.

## Why you would want it

`wwl`, which this catalog also carries, answers the same question in one line of text and is the better tool inside a script. This is the one to use when you want to see the path: pointing a beam, checking whether a claimed contact is plausible, or explaining to somebody why the short path goes over the pole.

## Before it will work

A desktop session. It talks to no hardware and needs no network.

## How it installs

- source (qmake) from https://www.qsl.net/on4qz/qgrid/downloads/qgrid_3_2.tgz
  - build dependencies: `build-essential`, `pkg-config`, `qtbase5-dev`, `qt5-qmake`, `qtbase5-dev-tools`, `qtmultimedia5-dev`
  - Built in a Debian 13 container on 2026-08-28: qmake exits 0, make exits 0, and `make install` exits 0 and puts the binary in place. AHRL lists libqt5widgets5 and libqt5multimediawidgets5 as build dependencies; those are runtime libraries and the build needs the -dev packages, which is what is listed here. **Its `.pro` hardcodes `target.path=/usr/local/bin`** rather than reading PREFIX, so a non-default prefix is silently ignored. Our default prefix is /usr/local, so this lands correctly today and would not if that changed — recorded rather than discovered later. It also declares a `dox` install target that runs doxygen over the manual; the install succeeds without doxygen present.

Binaries this produces:

- `qgrid`

## Known problems

Great-circle paths are the right answer for a beam heading and not always the path a signal took -- long path and skewed paths near the auroral zones are real and this does not model them. A six-character locator is a square several kilometres across, so distances between nearby stations carry inherent slop. Not packaged by any target, so source is the only route.
